statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a proper [model category](c:model-category) and $Q$ an endofunctor with a natural map $\eta\colon \mathrm{id}\to Q$ that keeps weak equivalences, makes $\eta_{QX}$ and $Q\eta_X$ weak equivalences, and keeps the [homotopy pullback](c:homotopy-pullback) squares of condition (A.6). Then $Q$-equivalences, $Q$-fibrations and the old cofibrations form a model structure on $\mathcal C$.

hypotheses.text: The functor $Q$ and the natural map $\eta\colon \mathrm{id}\to Q$ keep weak equivalences, and $\eta_{QX}$ and $Q\eta_X$ are weak equivalences.
The functor $Q$ keeps the [homotopy pullback](c:homotopy-pullback) squares of condition (A.6).

conclusion: The $Q$-equivalences ($Qf$ is a weak equivalence), the $Q$-fibrations (fibrations whose unit square is a homotopy pullback) and the cofibrations of $\mathcal C$ form a model structure.

proofs.name: Bousfield-Friedlander construction
proofs.slogan: Check the model category axioms for the new classes, using properness and the homotopy pullback condition.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline of Bousfield and Friedlander (Theorem A.7), with Bousfield's later version in Theorem 9.3. The long verification of the lifting property is cited, not repeated.

roles.why: Properness lets homotopy pullbacks respect weak equivalences, which every later step needs.
The conditions on $Q$ and $\eta$ make $Q$-equivalences satisfy two-out-of-three and contain all weak equivalences.
The pullback condition makes the factorization map a $Q$-fibration and gives the lifting property.

steps.slogan: Define the $Q$-equivalences and $Q$-fibrations and check two-out-of-three and retracts.
steps.detail: A $Q$-equivalence is a map $f$ with $Qf$ a weak equivalence, so two-out-of-three and closure under retracts follow from functoriality of $Q$. A $Q$-fibration is a fibration whose unit square is a homotopy pullback, and this class is closed under retracts too.

steps.slogan: Identify the new trivial fibrations with the trivial fibrations of $\mathcal C$.
steps.detail: A $Q$-fibration $f$ with $Qf$ a weak equivalence is a homotopy pullback of the weak equivalence $Qf$, so $f$ is a weak equivalence by properness. A trivial fibration of $\mathcal C$ is a $Q$-fibration because $Q$ keeps weak equivalences. So cofibrations lift against them, and every map factors as a cofibration followed by a trivial fibration.

steps.slogan: Factor each map as a $Q$-trivial cofibration followed by a $Q$-fibration.
steps.detail: Bousfield and Friedlander build this factorization from a factorization in $\mathcal C$ and a homotopy pullback along the unit $\eta$. Properness and the pullback condition show that the second map is a $Q$-fibration and the first map is a cofibration and a $Q$-equivalence.

steps.slogan: Show that $Q$-trivial cofibrations lift against $Q$-fibrations.
steps.detail: The first maps of the factorizations in step 3 have the lifting property against every $Q$-fibration; the proof uses properness and the pullback condition. A $Q$-trivial cofibration is a retract of such a map by the retract argument, so it has the lifting property too.

steps.slogan: Collect the axioms into a model structure on $\mathcal C$.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives the weak equivalence axioms, steps 2 and 3 give the two factorizations, and steps 2 and 4 give the two lifting properties. Every weak equivalence of $\mathcal C$ is a $Q$-equivalence and the cofibrations agree, so the structure is the left [Bousfield localization](c:bousfield-localization) at the $Q$-equivalences.

concepts.c:model-category: The theorem produces a new model structure on the same category.
concepts.c:homotopy-pullback: Q-fibrations are defined by a homotopy pullback square of the unit.
concepts.c:bousfield-localization: The new structure localizes the old one at the Q-equivalences.

source.ref: A. K. Bousfield and E. M. Friedlander, Homotopy theory of Gamma-spaces, spectra, and bisimplicial sets, in Geometric Applications of Homotopy Theory II, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 658, Springer, 1978, pp. 80-130 (Theorem A.7); see also A. K. Bousfield, On the telescoping homotopy theory of spaces, Transactions of the AMS 353 (2001), 2391-2426 (Theorem 9.3).
source.note: The five steps follow the verification of the model axioms in Appendix A of Bousfield and Friedlander; the lifting argument of step 4 and the factorization of step 3 are cited in full there.

statement: Let a symmetric $(v,k,\lambda)$ [block design](c:block-design) exist with $k<v$ and $\lambda\ge 1$: $v$ points, $v$ blocks, each block has $k$ points, each pair of points lies in $\lambda$ blocks. If $v$ is even, then $k-\lambda$ is a square. If $v$ is odd, then $x^2-(k-\lambda)y^2-(-1)^{(v-1)/2}\lambda z^2=0$ has a nontrivial integer solution.

hypotheses.text: A symmetric $(v,k,\lambda)$ [block design](c:block-design) exists: $v$ points, $v$ blocks, block size $k$, and $\lambda$ blocks through each pair of points.

conclusion: For even $v$ the number $k-\lambda$ is a square; for odd $v$ the equation $x^2-(k-\lambda)y^2-(-1)^{(v-1)/2}\lambda z^2=0$ has a nontrivial integer solution.

proofs.name: Rational equivalence of quadratic forms
proofs.slogan: The incidence matrix makes a quadratic form equivalent to a sum of squares over the rationals, and Witt cancellation turns this into a splitting quaternion algebra.
proofs.scope: All $v$ and $k$ of a nontrivial symmetric design. The even case uses only the determinant; the odd case splits by $v \bmod 4$.

roles.why: The design gives an integer matrix $N$ with $NN^T=nI+\lambda J$, where $n=k-\lambda$.
It gives $n>0$ and $k\ne0$, so the determinant is nonzero and Lagrange's theorem applies to $n$.

steps.slogan: Write the incidence equation and compute its determinant.
steps.detail: Let $N$ be the $v\times v$ [incidence](c:block-design) matrix and $n=k-\lambda$. Then $NN^T=nI+\lambda J$ and $\lambda(v-1)=k(k-1)$, so $n+\lambda v=k^2$ and $\det(NN^T)=n^{v-1}k^2$. Also $n>0$ because $k<v$.

steps.slogan: For even $v$, show that $n$ is a square.
steps.detail: The integer $\det N$ satisfies $(\det N)^2=n^{v-1}k^2$ with $k\ne0$, so $n^{v-1}$ is a rational square. The exponent $v-1$ is odd, so $n=n^{v-1}/(n^{(v-2)/2})^2$ is a rational square, hence an integer square.

steps.slogan: For odd $v$, split the form $nI+\lambda J$ along the all-ones vector.
steps.detail: Since $\det N\ne0$, the map $x\mapsto N^Tx$ shows that $q(x)=n|x|^2+\lambda(e\cdot x)^2$ is a [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) equivalent over $\mathbb Q$ to $I_v$, where $e=(1,\dots,1)$. On $e^\perp$ it equals $n|x|^2$, and $q(e)=vk^2$ by step 1. So $q\cong\langle v\rangle\perp r$ and $nI_v\cong\langle nv\rangle\perp r$ for one form $r$.

steps.slogan: Absorb the factor $n$ into four coordinates at a time.
steps.detail: By Lagrange's theorem $n=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$. Euler's identity gives an integer matrix $B$ with $B^TB=nI_4$, so $nI_4\cong I_4$ over $\mathbb Q$. Hence $nI_{4m}\cong I_{4m}$ for every $m$.

steps.slogan: Cancel the common form $r$ in the Witt group of $\mathbb Q$.
steps.detail: By Witt cancellation, step 3 gives $[r]=[I_v]-[\langle v\rangle]$ and $[nI_v]=[\langle nv\rangle]+[r]$. For $v\equiv1\pmod4$ step 4 gives $nI_v\cong I_{v-1}\perp\langle n\rangle$, so $\langle1,-n,-v,nv\rangle$ has class $0$. For $v\equiv3\pmod4$ use $nI_v\perp\langle n\rangle\cong I_{v+1}$; then $\langle1,-n,v,-nv\rangle$ has class $0$. So the [quaternion algebra](c:quaternion-algebra) $(n,v)$, respectively $(n,-v)$, splits over $\mathbb Q$.

steps.slogan: Combine the cases into the two stated conclusions.
steps.detail: For even $v$, step 2 is the claim. For odd $v$, $n\cdot1^2+\lambda v\cdot1^2=k^2$ splits $(n,\lambda v)$. Bimultiplicativity gives $(n,\lambda)=(n,\lambda v)(n,v)$ for $v\equiv1$ and $(n,-\lambda)=(n,\lambda v)(n,-v)$ for $v\equiv3\pmod 4$. Both are trivial, so $x^2-ny^2\mp\lambda z^2=0$ has a rational, hence an integer, nontrivial solution.

concepts.c:block-design: The design supplies the incidence matrix and the equation $NN^T=nI+\lambda J$.
concepts.c:quadratic-form: The proof compares two quadratic forms that are equivalent over the rationals.
concepts.c:quaternion-algebra: A split quaternion algebra is the same as a solvable conic.

source.note: The theorem is due to Bruck and Ryser (1949) and Chowla and Ryser (1950). This proof uses the incidence-matrix equation, four squares and Witt cancellation over the rationals.

statement: Let $1\le q<x$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$. The number $\pi(x;q,a)$ of [primes](c:prime-number) $p\le x$ in the [arithmetic progression](c:arithmetic-progression) $a \bmod q$ satisfies $\pi(x;q,a)\le \dfrac{2x}{\varphi(q)\log(x/q)}$.

hypotheses.text: The modulus $q$ and the bound $x$ satisfy $1\le q<x$.

proofs.name: Large sieve of Montgomery and Vaughan
proofs.slogan: Turn the progression into a sieve problem and bound the survivors with the large sieve inequality.
proofs.scope: An outline of Theorem 2 of Montgomery and Vaughan, which treats intervals $(x,x+y]$ and gives the stated bound for $[1,x]$. The explicit estimates of that paper are cited, not repeated.

roles.why: The condition $q<x$ makes the interval of $m$ long and keeps $\log(x/q)$ positive.
Coprimality means that no prime divisor of $q$ divides any term $a+qm$.

steps.slogan: Write the primes of the progression as $a+qm$ with $m$ in a short interval.
steps.detail: Each prime $p\le x$ with $p\equiv a\pmod q$ equals $a+qm$ with $0\le m\le x/q$, an interval of length $N\approx x/q$. Counting the $m$ for which $a+qm$ is [prime](c:prime-number) is a sieve problem.

steps.slogan: Remove one residue class modulo each prime $\ell\nmid q$ up to $Q$.
steps.detail: For a prime $\ell\le Q$ with $\ell\nmid q$, exactly one class of $m$ modulo $\ell$ has $\ell\mid a+qm$. For $\ell\mid q$ no class is removed, since $\gcd(a,q)=1$. A prime $a+qm>Q$ survives, so $\pi(x;q,a)$ is at most the number $Z$ of survivors plus $Q$.

steps.slogan: Apply the large sieve inequality to the survivors.
steps.detail: The arithmetic large sieve inequality of Montgomery and Vaughan bounds $Z$ by a quantity of size $(N+Q^2)/L$, where $L=\sum_{r\le Q,\,(r,q)=1}\mu^2(r)/\varphi(r)$ for this sieve with one removed class per prime.

steps.slogan: Bound the sum $L$ from below by $\frac{\varphi(q)}{q}\log Q$.
steps.detail: Since $1/\varphi(r)=\sum_{\mathrm{rad}(n)=r}1/n$, $L\ge\sum_{n\le Q,(n,q)=1}1/n$. Splitting off the part of $n$ built from primes dividing $q$ shows that this sum is at least $\frac{\varphi(q)}{q}\sum_{n\le Q}1/n\ge\frac{\varphi(q)}{q}\log Q$.

steps.slogan: Choose $Q$ in terms of $x/q$ to obtain the constant $2$.
steps.detail: The choice of $Q$ balances $N$ against $Q^2$: $Q^2$ is of smaller order than $N$ while $\log Q$ stays close to $\frac12\log N$, which gives the factor $2$. Montgomery and Vaughan treat all ranges of $x/q$ with explicit estimates, which gives the bound for every $q<x$.

concepts.c:prime-number: The proof counts the primes that survive the sieve.
concepts.c:arithmetic-progression: The primes of the progression $a \bmod q$ become the integers $a+qm$ to be sieved.

source.ref: H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, The large sieve, Mathematika 20 (1973), 119-134 (Theorem 2).
source.note: Montgomery and Vaughan derive the bound from their large sieve inequality; steps 3 and 5 rest on the inequality and the explicit estimates of that paper.

statement: In ZF set theory no [set](c:set) has exactly the [von Neumann ordinals](c:is-ordinal) as its elements. Equivalently, the class of all ordinals is a proper class, and by separation no set contains every ordinal.

hypotheses.text: Sets obey the axioms of ZF, in particular separation and foundation.

conclusion: No [set](c:set) $x$ satisfies $y\in x \iff y$ is an ordinal.

formal.difference: mathlib states that the class of ordinals is not an element of the class of all sets, which means that it is not a set. It defines an ordinal as a transitive set with transitive membership, which agrees with the well-order definition.

proofs.name: The set of ordinals would be an ordinal
proofs.slogan: A set of all ordinals would itself be an ordinal, so it would belong to itself.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. A set containing every ordinal gives a set with exactly the ordinals as elements by separation, so only the second form is proved.

roles.why: Separation reduces the statement to exact sets of ordinals, and foundation forbids a set that belongs to itself.

steps.slogan: Assume that a set $x$ has exactly the ordinals as elements.
steps.detail: Suppose $x$ is a [set](c:set) with $y\in x$ if and only if $y$ is a [von Neumann ordinal](c:is-ordinal), that is, a transitive set on which membership is transitive. The aim is to show that $x$ is itself an ordinal.

steps.slogan: Show that $x$ is a transitive set.
steps.detail: Let $z\in y\in x$. Then $y$ is an ordinal, and every element of an ordinal is an ordinal, so $z$ is an ordinal and $z\in x$. Hence every element of $x$ is a subset of $x$.

steps.slogan: Show that membership is transitive on the elements of $x$.
steps.detail: Let $u\in v$ and $v\in w$ with $w\in x$. The set $w$ is an ordinal, so its membership relation is transitive, and $u\in w$. Under foundation a transitive set with this property is an ordinal.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $x$ is an ordinal with $x\in x$, which foundation forbids.
steps.detail: By steps 2 and 3, $x$ is an ordinal. Since $x$ has all ordinals as elements, $x\in x$. This contradicts foundation, which says that no set is an element of itself. So no such set exists.

concepts.c:set: The theorem says that the ordinals do not form a set.
concepts.c:is-ordinal: The assumed set is shown to be an ordinal, which gives the contradiction.

source.note: mathlib shows that a set whose members are the ordinals is transitive (IsOrdinal.mem) with transitive membership (IsOrdinal.mem_trans), so it is an ordinal that belongs to itself, against ZFClass.cmem_irrefl.

statement: Let $n\ge2$ and let $u>0$ be [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) on the punctured unit ball $B\setminus\{0\}\subset\mathbb R^n$. Then $u=bE+h$ on $B\setminus\{0\}$, where $b\ge0$, $h$ is harmonic on $B$, and $E$ is the [fundamental solution](c:fundamental-solution): $E(x)=|x|^{2-n}$ for $n\ge3$ and $E(x)=\log(1/|x|)$ for $n=2$.

hypotheses.text: The function $u$ is [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) on the punctured ball $B\setminus\{0\}$ in $\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge2$.

conclusion: There are a constant $b\ge0$ and a harmonic function $h$ on $B$ with $u=bE+h$ on $B\setminus\{0\}$.

proofs.name: Spherical means and harmonic expansion
proofs.slogan: Subtract a Poisson integral, show that the remainder is a multiple of the Green function plus a removable part, and remove the singularity.
proofs.scope: The unit ball and every $n\ge2$. The construction fixes a radius $r<1$, and the result passes from $B_r$ to $B$ in the last step.

roles.why: Positivity gives $w\ge0$ near $0$ and lets Harnack's inequality bound $w$ by its mean.
[Harmonicity](c:harmonic-function) makes the spherical means radial harmonic and allows the expansion in spherical harmonics.

steps.slogan: Subtract the Poisson integral of $u$ on a sphere $|x|=r<1$.
steps.detail: Let $v$ be the Poisson integral of $u$ on $|x|=r$: harmonic on $B_r$ and continuous on its closure. Put $w=u-v$ on $B_r\setminus\{0\}$; then $w=0$ on $|x|=r$.

steps.slogan: Show that $w\ge0$ by the minimum principle with a small multiple of $E$.
steps.detail: For $\varepsilon>0$ the function $w+\varepsilon E$ is harmonic. It tends to $+\infty$ at $0$ because $u>0$ and $v$ is bounded, and it is $\ge0$ on $|x|=r$ because $E>0$ there. The minimum principle on small annuli gives $w+\varepsilon E\ge0$; let $\varepsilon\to0$.

steps.slogan: Compute the spherical mean of $w$ as a multiple of $E-E(r)$.
steps.detail: The spherical mean $M(\rho)$ of $w$ on $|x|=\rho$ is radial and harmonic, so $M=\alpha+\beta E(\rho)$. Since $M(r)=0$, $M\ge0$ and $E(\rho)\to\infty$ as $\rho\to0$, we get $\alpha=-\beta E(r)$ and $\beta\ge0$. Put $G=E-E(r)$, so $M=\beta G$.

steps.slogan: Bound $w$ by its spherical mean with Harnack's inequality and subtract.
steps.detail: Harnack's inequality on the annulus $\rho/2<|x|<2\rho$ gives $w(x)\le C\,M(|x|)$ for $|x|<r/2$, with $C$ depending only on $n$. Then $g=w-\beta G$ is harmonic, has all spherical means $0$, and satisfies $|g|\le(C+1)\beta E$ near $0$.

steps.slogan: Expand $g$ in spherical harmonics and show that $g$ extends harmonically across $0$.
steps.detail: The coefficient of a degree-$k$ spherical harmonic is $a\rho^k+b\rho^{2-n-k}$ for $k\ge1$, and it is $0$ for $k=0$ because all means vanish. The bound $|g|\le CE$ forces $b=0$, since $\rho^{2-n-k}/E(\rho)\to\infty$. So $g$ is a convergent sum of harmonic polynomials and extends harmonically to $B_r$.

steps.slogan: Assemble $u=\beta E+h$ and extend $h$ to the whole ball.
steps.detail: On $B_r\setminus\{0\}$, $u=v+\beta G+g=\beta E+h$ with $h=v-\beta E(r)+g$ harmonic on $B_r$. The function $u-\beta E$ is harmonic on $B\setminus\{0\}$ and equals $h$ near $0$, so it extends to a harmonic function on $B$. Take $b=\beta$.

concepts.c:harmonic-function: All the objects $u$, $v$, $w$ and $g$ are harmonic, and their means are radial harmonic.
concepts.c:fundamental-solution: The singular part of $u$ is a multiple of the fundamental solution $E$.

source.note: The classical proof of Bôcher's theorem, as in Axler, Bourdon and Ramey, Harmonic Function Theory (2nd ed., Springer, 2001), in the chapter on positive harmonic functions.
